assertion_analysis.fails_if: The command rule is dropped and a port list is read as jobs: ['nc','-z','a-host','50000,50001'] stops returning ().
The port-ceiling override is dropped, so ['nc','-z','a-host','70000,70001'] returns () instead of the two ids.
The command rule is over-applied to every command, so a script handed '1234,5678' stops naming two jobs.
The raw-vector flag read is removed: --jobs=..., and -j..., return only the first id, as the reversed reader arm records.
Only the word-split id is queried, so the fixture with the script idle and _scheduler_stub listing BATCH_JOBS[1] is classified producer-gone instead of waiting.

assertion_independence: every expected value is a literal or a module constant read from outside the code under test (the port pair, the 70000 pair, the 1234/5678 pair, PRODUCER_GONE_STATUS, BATCH_JOBS as the fixture's declared ids); the two BATCH_JOBS round trips compare the reader's output against the same constant that built the probe, which is a literal in disguise and still reddens when an id is dropped, so no assertion moves with the code it judges.

0.reason: non-blocking edge case noted by the re-review; tracked as a follow-up, not this section's endpoint

findings.text: non-blocking: a comma-separated job batch reached through a shell or interpreter string is still unread, because the job-shaped list is applied only to the raw probe items and never to the words the shell or interpreter string is split into: ['bash','-lc','python x.py 1234,5678'] and ['ssh','host','python x.py 1234,5678'] both return (), so a run whose probe passes its jobs that way can still read producer-gone while a job is alive. This delta does not introduce the gap (the same loop ran over probe[1:] before it) and the declared canonical shape is a shell-free interpreter vector, so it does not hold this node; the fix is not a one-liner because command_takes_ports must then derive from the inner command, not the shell.
